passage: I am Anjali. Joseph and I had been together four months when he began saying it: "If you really loved me, you would." Sometimes he said it softly, sometimes as a joke, once with his jaw tight, outside my gate after a film. I kept apologising, and hated that I was apologising. That night I sat on my bed with a knot in my stomach, wondering whether he would leave. Next day I told my friend Rekha, who said, "Love that makes you scared to say no isn't a test you have to pass." So I told Joseph plainly that I set my own pace and that no meant no. He went quiet and said he needed to think. I still don't know how it will end. But for the first time in weeks I could breathe.

qa.q: How long had Anjali and Joseph been together when he began saying it?
qa.a: They had been together four months.

qa.q: What was Anjali afraid of on the night Anjali sat on the bed?
qa.a: Anjali was afraid Joseph would leave if Anjali said no. The knot in Anjali's stomach and the constant apologising show fear and self-doubt.

qa.q: What could Anjali do if Joseph keeps pressuring Anjali?
qa.a: Anjali could keep saying no plainly, keep talking to Rekha or another trusted person, and remember that someone who respects Anjali accepts a no.

qa.q: How might Rekha see Anjali's situation?
qa.a: Rekha sees a friend being made to feel scared, and points out that love should not make someone afraid to say no.

grounding: A partner says 'if you loved me you would', and the protagonist decides their own pace and talks to a trusted friend.

passage:
Ramesh,
I'm writing this because when we talk, I lose my words.
On Saturday, when I said I wasn't ready to stay the night at your flat, you went quiet and then said, "If you really loved me, you wouldn't make me wait." I've heard some version of it three times now. Each time I feel guilty, then scared you'll leave, then angry that I feel scared.
So here it is, clearly. I do care about you. And I decide my own pace. Being ready is not a test of love. If you respect me, a "not yet" has to be okay without sulking or asking again the next day.
I told my friend Kokila about this yesterday. She asked whether I feel safe saying no to you. I want the answer to be yes. That part is up to you now.
Hansa

qa.q: What did Ramesh say on Saturday?
qa.a: "If you really loved me, you wouldn't make me wait."

qa.q: What mix of feelings does Hansa describe each time Ramesh says it?
qa.a: Hansa feels guilty, then scared that Ramesh will leave, then angry about feeling scared.

qa.q: What else, besides the letter, can help Hansa if the pressure continues?
qa.a: Keep talking with Kokila, the trusted friend who asked whether Hansa feels safe saying no, so Hansa isn't facing it alone.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Possibly defensive or embarrassed at first, but the letter gives Ramesh a clear choice: accept "not yet" or show that Hansa's pace isn't respected.

grounding: Shows a partner using love as pressure to go further, and the wise stance that one decides one's own pace and can lean on a trusted friend.

passage:
You asked why I've been so quiet, Rhea, so let me just say it. Parveen and I broke up on Sunday.
For weeks Parveen kept saying the same thing: "If you really loved me, you'd stop holding back." I almost gave in. Honestly, I almost did it just so I wouldn't lose Parveen. I'd lie awake thinking, is something wrong with me for not being ready?
On Sunday, in the park near college, I said it out loud: "I'm not ready, and I'm not going to be pushed." Parveen said, "Then this isn't love," and walked off.
And you know what, Rhea? I cried the whole auto ride home, but under the crying I felt light. Someone who respected me would have waited. I'm glad I didn't trade myself away to keep them.
So yes, this is me, Aparna, single and sad and weirdly proud. Now tell me about your week.

qa.q: When did Aparna and Parveen break up?
What was Aparna afraid of while the pressure went on?
qa.a: Aparna was afraid of losing Parveen and anxious that something was wrong with not being ready, lying awake over it.

qa.q: What helped Aparna most, and what could help sooner if pressure like this returns?
qa.a: Saying clearly "I'm not ready, and I'm not going to be pushed"; talking to a trusted friend like Rhea early on would add support.

qa.q: How does Parveen seem to see Aparna's "not ready"?
qa.a: As proof of not being loved ("Then this isn't love"), treating Aparna's pace as a failure rather than a boundary.

grounding: Illustrates pressure framed as a test of love, the pull to give in from fear of loss, and choosing one's own pace.
